title: Template Method pattern
idea: The Template Method pattern fixes an algorithm's steps in a final base-class method and lets subclasses fill in only the steps that vary.
points: The base class owns the order and shared rules; subclasses supply the abstract steps.
A hook is an optional step with a default body that subclasses may override.
In the JDK, `AbstractList` builds iteration and `indexOf` on your `get` and `size`.
It binds variation at compile time through inheritance; prefer Strategy for runtime swaps.

hero.title: One export call, in fixed order

items.label: 1 · validate
items.text: Base class: `requireNonNull` on the list. No subclass can skip it.

items.label: 2 · header()
items.text: Abstract step. CSV writes a column line; Markdown writes a table head.

items.label: 3 · filter
items.text: Base class drops rows with a negative quantity, for every format.

items.label: 4 · row(s)
items.text: Abstract step, called once for each kept sale.

items.label: 5 · footer()
items.text: Hook: empty by default. Only Markdown overrides it to add a total.

code.title: The problem: copy-paste
code.caption: Two exporters copied from each other. A business rule survives in only one.

walk.text: The CSV report drops negative rows. That is a business rule, not a format detail.
The Markdown copy kept the loop and the shape but lost the filter.
Same data, two formats, two answers: the bad row appears only in Markdown.
Even the trimming is duplicated. Every shared fix must be made in every copy.

code.title: The fix: template method
code.caption: One final method fixes the order; subclasses fill in the format steps.

walk.text: `final` locks the order. No subclass can override `export` and skip validation.
Shared steps live here once: the null check, the row filter and the total.
Abstract steps: the compiler forces every exporter to supply a header and a row.
A hook has a default body, so `CsvExporter` can ignore it.
Markdown overrides both steps and the hook to add a total line.
The caller sees only `ReportExporter`, so each subclass is a drop-in replacement.

pitfalls: Leaving the template method non-final lets a subclass reorder or skip the shared steps.
Calling overridable steps from a constructor runs subclass code before its fields are set.
Several layers of abstract templates scatter one algorithm across files; keep the hierarchy shallow.

quiz.q: Each request picks its header style and row format independently at runtime. What fits best?
options: One Template Method subclass per header and row mix
Inject header and row Strategies into one exporter
Make `export` non-final so callers override it
Add a format flag and a `switch` inside `row`
quiz.why: Template Method fixes each choice per subclass at compile time. Independent runtime choices belong to Strategy; subclasses would multiply for every combination.

takeaway: The base class fixes the order; subclasses fill in the blanks.
